title: U.S. and China Set Up AI Hotline After Three-Day Summit
summary: What happens when the world's two biggest economies can't talk? Small problems can turn into big ones. That's why the U.S. and China spent three days in Washington, D.C., trying to keep the lines open. On Saturday, the two governments announced they will create a special channel for handling AI-related incidents and speed up work on military crisis communications. The summit between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump didn't produce any giant breakthroughs, but analysts say the new working groups are important because they could stop disputes from escalating (getting worse). "Personal diplomacy between the two leaders is important, but the emphasis on working-level engagement, military-to-military dialogue and crisis-management mechanisms suggests an effort to make that stability more durable and institutionalized," said Wang Zichen of the Center for China and Globalization in Beijing. On trade, the two sides agreed to extend a truce on tariffs (taxes on imports) by two months and to keep reducing tariffs on about $30 billion worth of goods — mostly non-sensitive items like agricultural products and holiday decorations. China also agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the U.S. in 2027 and 2028. But Trump made it clear the U.S. won't slow down its AI work. "We're leading by at least a year, maybe a year and a half," he told reporters. "I would rather not integrate because we're leading by a lot." Both countries also said Iran should honor its promise not to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country should charge tolls on international waterways — likely a reference to the Strait of Hormuz. They will meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November.
why_it_matters: When the two largest economies stop talking, small disagreements over trade or technology can spiral into decisions that raise prices and reshape entire industries — so the new hotlines and working groups matter most for how stable the next few years will be for everyone else.

background_read: The United States and China are the world's two largest economies, so how they get along affects prices, jobs and technology almost everywhere. Their last big tariff fight began in 2018, when both sides taxed hundreds of billions of dollars of each other's goods before signing a limited 'phase one' deal in early 2020.

Xi Jinping (China's president) and Donald Trump (the U.S. president) are the two leaders at the center of this meeting. Working groups and hotlines are an old diplomatic tool: after the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, Washington and Moscow set up a direct 'hotline' so leaders could reach each other instantly instead of guessing.

APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) is a yearly gathering of Pacific-region economies that started in 1989 and often hosts side meetings between leaders. Shenzhen, the city hosting this November's summit, is a major technology and manufacturing hub in southern China near Hong Kong.

perspectives.description: Analysts see the AI channel and military-to-military talks as real progress: they turn a friendly relationship between two leaders into permanent machinery that keeps working even when relations get rocky. Supporters argue that steady, lower-level contact prevents small incidents from becoming crises.

The summit produced no major deals: tariffs were only paused, not removed, and Trump openly said he would rather not cooperate on AI. Critics say that without deeper agreements on technology and trade, the hotline is a thin layer of politeness over a rivalry that keeps growing.

Great-power rivals have long built communication channels like the Cold War hotline precisely because they remain rivals. From this angle, the deal is less about friendship and more about managing competition safely, which is why low-level working groups often outlast leader-to-leader goodwill.

The real test comes at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, when the two sides must decide whether to extend the tariff truce again and whether the AI channel expands into shared safety rules. If talks stall, both countries will keep racing ahead on AI and trade on their own terms.
